holds the templates, the language definition and the CEDM specification, with
the `loco new` scaffold skipped. That is how the website hands over a whole
application as a `.zip`; `scripts/sites/build-site-bundles.ts` in the
`app-with-ai-rust` copy builds it, and a comparison against `appwithai generate`
over every published model holds it to the same files.

### 4.2 Compilation map

| Model input | Compiler | Output in the generated app |
|---|---|---|
| `entities`, `relationships` | `compileErdRecords` | bus-table DDL, the dictionary seed, forms, grids, request suites |
| an entity's `indexes` | same pass | real DDL indexes in the bus-table migration |
| `enums`, an attribute's `enum` | same pass | bound enums → typed columns + UI selects (`sys_ref_list`, or a table) |
| `categories` | `compileCategoryDeclarations` | dashboard groups (`sys_category`) |
| `rules` (`nodes`, `edges`) | `compileRuleDeclarations` → `rules/jdm-converter.ts` | JDM graph → `sys_rule_definitions` |
| a rule's `actions` | same | JDM decision table → rule actions |
| `hooks` | `compileHookDeclarations` | handler modules + registry around every CRUD op |
| `stateMachines` | `compileWorkflows` | `sys_workflow_transitions`, enforced on every status write |
| `sagas` | `compileSagaDeclarations` | BPMN → `sys_workflow_definitions`, one service task per step |
| `rbac` | `compileRbacDeclarations` | `sys_operation_access` + `sys_transition_access`, enforced by the access guard |
| `reports` | `compileReportDeclarations` | `sys_report`, served at `/api/reports` |

**A category needs a `name`.** The schema requires it, so a category without one
is an error at its line rather than a grouping that silently falls into the
default `General` category.

### 4.3 Templates — the Loco backend, the front end and the test suites

```
packages/generator/templates/
├── common/                 12 .hbs — migrations, seeds, hooks, services shared by the stack
└── tanstack-astryx-loco/
    ├── docker-compose.yml.hbs     rendered; branches on --db (no postgres service for neon)
    ├── backend/   105 .hbs — the Loco crate: Cargo workspace + Cargo.lock, migration/
    │                         crate (m0000–m0019 and the bus tables), config/*.yaml,
    │                         controllers (bus, sys, auth, me, rules, workflow, audit,
    │                         records, reports, jobs, ai), services (dictionary,
    │                         dynamic_repo, row_json, authz, promotion, workflow),
    │                         tasks (seed_dictionary, seed_workflows, seed_access,
    │                         seed_reports, ensure_admin), src/openapi.rs, and the
    │                         request test suites
    ├── frontend/   71 .hbs — TanStack Start routes and components, the Astryx overlay
    │                         (all components/ui adapters), i18n, the manual
    └── tests/      36 .hbs — the bun:test harness and suites (§4.4)
```

The counts move. Treat them as the shape of the tree rather than a fact to
quote back — `find packages/generator/templates -name '*.hbs' | wc -l` is the
answer at any given moment.

**`loco new` does the scaffolding; the templates fill the rest.** Phase 1 shells
out to the Loco CLI (installing it if missing) in a scratch directory and copies
its output across — the framework's own CI workflow, `.rustfmt.toml`,
`AGENTS.md` — then prunes the starter files this architecture replaces. Phase 2
overlays the templates. `--skip-cli-scaffold` skips phase 1 for offline builds.

Adding a template: create the `.hbs`, register it in `RENDERED_FILES` in **both**
`loco-backend.generator.ts` and `crates/appwithai-gen/src/backend.rs` (or in the
front end's static-copy list for a verbatim file), supply context in the
generator's `prepareContext()` — **then generate an app and build it.** Templates
are `.hbs` text until rendered, so `bun run type-check` in this repository proves
nothing about them, and Handlebars strict mode is off in both engines: a helper
missing from one of them renders as an empty string.

### 4.4 The generated test suites

Every generated application ships two independent end-to-end suites over the
same HTTP surface. Both are generated from the model, so both grow when it does.

**`backend/tests/` — the Rust request suites, the primary gate.** `LOCO_ENV=test
cargo test --test app` against `<crate>_test`: a `crud_<entity>` and a
`rules_<entity>` suite per entity, plus shared suites for authentication,
the dictionary, permissions, `rbac`, rules, transitions, sagas, reports, jobs,
records, the OpenAPI document and the request log. `requests/permissions.rs`
sends no credentials at all and `requests/rbac.rs` builds a genuinely
non-master caller — every other suite signs in as the master-role administrator,
which passes every gate, so those two are the only ones that can see a hole in
access control.

**`tests/` — the bun:test suites**, driven by `run.ts`:

| | Asserts |
|---|---|
| `00-health`, `01-auth` | the app is up and a session works |
| `02-dictionary` | every column the model declared reached `sys_column` |
| `02b-dictionary-layout` | every entity has a window, a tab under it, and a field per column — a missing `sys_field` row errors nowhere, it just renders a form without that input |
| `02c-dictionary-references` | every column resolves to a control: dropdowns carry their enum values, lookups carry a target table and a label column |
| `03-crud.<entity>` | CRUD per entity |
| `04-bulk-seed` | volume, and that a re-run against a populated database still inserts |
| `05-rules.<entity>` | the rules bound to each entity |
| `06-rules-workflow`, `06b-workflow-transitions` | rules firing workflows; and that every transition a state machine declares is accepted and every move it does not is refused |
| `07`, `09` | random and multi-step workflow runs |
| `08-users-roles` | roles and what they may reach |
| `09-browser-volume` | 100k records through real Chromium (`--browser-volume`) |
| `10-benchmark`, `11-performance-budget` | measures and reports; then asserts on *ratios* (deep page vs first page, filtered vs unfiltered), which survive the change of machine that an absolute millisecond does not |

**`harness/model.ts` is the point of the newer suites.** It carries the model's
own enum values and state-machine transitions into the assertions. A suite that
reads the running application's dictionary and then asserts against that same
dictionary proves only that the application is self-consistent — it passes just
as happily when the generator dropped a value on the floor.

**Run it with `run.ts`**, which the generated `package.json` exposes as
`bun run test:e2e` (and `test:e2e:attach` for a backend that is already up):

```
bun run run.ts                  # everything, in order, 1000 records/entity
bun run run.ts --small          # 10 records — a smoke run
bun run run.ts --records 250    # an arbitrary volume
bun run run.ts --fast           # skip the bulk-seed volume suite
bun run run.ts --only crud      # substring filter on suite file names
bun run run.ts --no-server      # attach to a backend already listening
```

Do **not** suggest a bare `bun test` over the whole directory. The suites are
ordered (seed before rules before workflows) and `run.ts` gives each one its own
process, so a crash in one cannot take the rest down; run together they interfere,
and *which* test fails moves between runs. Prefer `cargo test` as the regression
gate — it covers the same ground in a quarter of the time and needs no separate
process; reach for the bun suites when a failure needs a readable HTTP
transcript.

The suites leave their rows behind on purpose, so a re-run against a populated
database is the normal case. Unique values are salted with a per-run token
(`E2E_RUN_TOKEN`, printed at the top of every run); set it to reproduce a run.

---

## 5. The generated application

### 5.1 Layout

```
generated-projects/<name>/
├── backend/    the Loco crate — API on :3000
│   ├── src/{controllers,services,models,tasks,hooks}, openapi.rs, app.rs
│   ├── migration/   the migration crate (raw SQL under migration/sql)
│   ├── seed/        dictionary.sql, workflows.sql, access.sql, reports.sql, rules.sql
│   ├── config/      development.yaml, production.yaml, test.yaml
│   └── tests/       the Rust request suites (§4.4)
├── frontend/   TanStack Start + Astryx — :3001
│   ├── src/{routes,components,hooks,contexts,providers,i18n,lib}
│   └── public/manual.html   the generated manual (see 5.6)
├── tests/      the bun:test E2E suite, driven by its own run.ts (see 4.4)
├── model/      model.eml.yaml — the model it was generated from, byte for byte
├── cedm/       the common CEDM specification the model draws on
└── docker-compose.yml, package.json, README.md
```

`cargo` owns `backend/` and `bun` owns `frontend/` and `tests/`; the backend has
no `package.json`. `cargo loco` is an alias the crate's `.cargo/config.toml`
defines (`run --bin <name>-cli --`), so `cargo loco db migrate`, `cargo loco db
seed` and `cargo loco start` work without installing anything. The database is
`<crate>_development`, which `cargo loco db migrate` does not create.

### 5.2 Database — three families

**`bus_*`** — one table per model entity (`bus_lead`, `bus_account`, …). Your
data.

**`sys_*`** — the Application Dictionary and platform tables:

| Table | Holds |
|---|---|
| `sys_table`, `sys_column` | every table and column: type, length, mandatory, unique, FK target |
| `sys_window`, `sys_tab`, `sys_field`, `sys_field_group` | how each entity is presented |
| `sys_element`, `sys_reference`, `sys_ref_list`, `sys_ref_table` | shared labels and lookups |
| `sys_role`, `sys_user`, `sys_user_roles`, `sys_access` | roles, users, and which windows a role may open |
| `sys_operation_access`, `sys_transition_access` | what `rbac` compiles to: per-operation and per-transition role restrictions |
| `sys_workflow_transitions` | valid moves from `stateMachines`; guard returns 403 for any status write that crosses no declared edge, for every caller including the master role. Read them at `GET /api/workflows/transitions` |
| `sys_rule_definitions` | seeded JDM rules |
| `sys_workflow_definitions` | seeded BPMN; automations live here too, not in a table of their own |
| `sys_workflow_runs` | one row per workflow execution |
| `sys_audit_log`, `sys_change_log` | audit trail |
| `sys_category` | dashboard grouping from `categories` |
| `sys_report_designs` | one default AnkaReport layout per entity; drives the Print button and Admin → Report Designs (see 5.7) |
| `sys_session`, `sys_val_rule` | sessions, validation rules |
| `sys_note` | user notes on records, append-only |
| `sys_system` | database-backed runtime configuration: AI endpoints, feature toggles, rate limits, logging, CORS, and application identity (`APP_NAME`, `APP_DESCRIPTION`). Fallback chain: DB row (active + non-empty) -> `process.env` -> hardcoded default. Administrators edit it from Admin > System Configuration; `APP_DESCRIPTION` renders as a textarea for a multi-paragraph application summary that appears in the manual and the dashboard header |

**auth tables** — Better Auth.

### 5.3 The Application Dictionary — why screens are data

Borrowed from Compiere ERP. Three layers:

| Layer | Holds | Comes from |
|---|---|---|
| Table & Column | every table and its columns | your `entities` |
| Window / Tab / Field | one window per entity, a tab per record view, a field per displayed column, with order and grouping | derived from the columns |
| Role | which windows a role may reach, and whether read-only | seeded, then yours |

**Consequence for any UI question**: there is no per-entity page component to
edit. A column marked mandatory in `sys_column` is required in every form; a
column with a reference renders as a lookup rather than a free-text box. To
change a screen, change the model and regenerate, or change the dictionary row
in `/admin`. Do not go looking for `LeadForm.tsx` — it does not exist.

### 5.4 Backend API

Global prefix `/api`. Every controller returns JSON; the backend renders no HTML.

| Route | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GET/POST /api/bus/{entity}`, `GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE /api/bus/{entity}/{id}` | generic CRUD for every entity the dictionary describes |
| `GET /api/bus/{entity}/meta`, `/fields/{form,grid}` | dictionary metadata and the field definitions driving the UI |
| `GET /api/bus/{entity}/lookup/{column}` | a lookup's rows, narrowed by the values the record passes |
| `/api/sys/{segment}[/{id}]`, `/api/sys/fields/batch-reorder`, `/api/sys/categories/…` | dictionary reads (open) and writes (master role) |
| `GET /api/me/dashboard`, `/api/me/permissions`, `/api/me/health` | the caller-scoped front page, what this caller may open, a readiness probe |
| `/api/rules`, `/api/rules/{id}/history`, `/api/rules/validate`, `/dry-run`, `/evaluate` | rules admin |
| `/api/workflow`, `/api/workflow/{id}/execute`, `/runs`, `/entity/{entity}/{id}` | workflow definitions and runs |
| `GET /api/workflow/transitions[?table=&from=]` | the state-machine edges the model declared |
| `/api/audit`, `/api/audit/{id}/verify` | the hash-chained audit trail |
| `/api/records/{entity}/{id}/{history,notes}` | a record's history and notes |
| `GET /api/reports`, `/api/reports/{name}/run` | the model's `reports`, run read-only |
| `/api/jobs/{kind}` | background jobs |
| `POST /api/ai/query` | the natural-language query |
| `/api/auth/{register,login,me,logout,change-password}` | sign-in (a JWT in an HttpOnly cookie, or a Bearer header) |
| `GET /api/v1/shape` | Electric sync |

`/api/bus/*` is authorised, not only authenticated: one `principal()` lookup per
request, then `sys_access`, the model's `rbac` operation rules, and — on a status
write — the drawn transitions, which bind everyone including the master role.
The application describes itself at `/openapi.json`, with `/redoc` and `/scalar`.

Accounts are **administrator-created by design** — a generated back-office app
has no self-service signup.

### 5.5 Frontend

TanStack Start + Astryx, file-based routing, dynamic segments use `$`:

```
routes/
├── dashboard.tsx              the categories, scoped to the reader
├── <entity>.tsx, <entity>.$id.tsx   per-entity list, and a record (id `new` creates)
├── $entity.tsx, $entity.$id.tsx     the generic, dictionary-driven fallbacks
├── reports.index.tsx, reports.$name.tsx, ask.tsx
├── auth/login.tsx
└── admin/
    ├── window/$windowId/tab/$tabId/field/$fieldId.tsx   dictionary editors
    ├── table/$tableId/column/$columnId.tsx, elements.tsx, references.tsx
    ├── categories.tsx, roles.tsx, users.tsx, system.tsx, audit.tsx
    ├── rules/{index,new,$id.edit}.tsx, automations.tsx
    └── workflow-definitions/{index,new,$id.edit}.tsx
```



The dashboard is your `categories`: one block per category, heading
and description taken from the model. A final block, Application Dictionary, is
the generator's own admin surface. Above them is a **Manual** button.

**Both halves are scoped to the reader, and neither is a fixed list.** The
entity blocks hold what the `rbac` `read` entries let this role see, with line items
excluded because a child is reached through its parent; a category whose every
entity belongs to someone else does not appear at all. The Application
Dictionary block is the admin windows this role is granted through `sys_access`,
so an administrator and an ordinary user see different cards there — and a
window the dictionary defines is never withheld for want of an icon. Every
card's icon comes from the dictionary: `sys_category.icon` for a heading,
`sys_table.icon` for an entity, `sys_window.icon` for an admin card.

### 5.6 The manual

Generation writes **one self-contained HTML page** describing the application it
just produced: a contents menu, then a section per entity giving every field with
its control type, its constraints, its enumerated values and its help text,
followed by that entity's relationships, its state machine, the rules that fire
on it and the roles allowed to read it — then the rules, the processes, and how
the application was built.

| | |
|---|---|
| Rendered by | `packages/generator/src/manual/index.ts`, from the `ParsedModel` |
| Generated application | `frontend/public/manual.html`, served at `/manual.html`, and in the downloadable `.zip` |
| Linked from | the **Manual** button on both dashboards |

No stylesheet, no script, no font, no image — it is served by a Service Worker,
by a static directory and by a `file://` double-click out of a zip, and one file
with its CSS inline is the only form that survives all three.

#### What the manual derives automatically

Most of the manual requires no help text at all — it is read directly from the
model's structure. The table below shows what each subsection of an entity
section contains and where it comes from:

| Subsection | What it shows | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Opening paragraph | Business description of the entity | the entity's `help` — blank placeholder if omitted |
| **Fields** — control type | How the field renders (text input, select, date picker, switch, textarea, lookup, …) | Derived from the attribute's type (referenceId): int → number, bool → switch, `fk` → lookup, string with `enum` → select, etc. |
| **Fields** — constraints | Mandatory, unique, max length | Derived from attribute flags and length |
| **Fields** — enumerated values | List of allowed values with labels | `enums` + the attribute's `enum` + `sys_ref_list` |
| **Fields** — purpose | Why the field exists, what value is expected | the attribute's `help` — dash if omitted |
| **Relationships** | What entities this one links to and from, with cardinality | `relationships` and `fk` columns |
| **Lifecycle** | State machine table: From state / To state / Trigger | `stateMachines` transitions |
| **Rules and automation** | Decision rules, sagas, hooks that fire on this entity | `rules`, `sagas`, `hooks` |
| **Access** | Roles allowed to read, create, update, delete | `rbac` entries |

The global sections at the end of the manual (all rules, all processes, how the
application was built, which tools were used) are also entirely automatic.

**The only text a model author controls is an entity's `help` and an
attribute's `help`**. A field with no `help` prints a dash in the
Purpose column; an entity with none gets a placeholder sentence as its lede. The
manual cannot describe an entity that does not exist or miss one that does — it
can only fail to explain them, and that failure is visible to every reader.

#### Writing an entity's `help` — guidance for language models

Write one or two sentences that answer: *what business role does this entity
play, and when does a record of this type come into existence?*

```yaml
entities:
  - name: Lead
    help: A prospective customer contact captured from marketing, events or direct outreach. A lead becomes an opportunity once a sales representative qualifies it.
  - name: SupportCase
    help: A reported problem or request from a customer. Each case tracks the issue from first contact through resolution and any follow-up.
  - name: Invoice
    help: A formal payment request issued to a customer account. Created on order dispatch; marked paid when settlement is confirmed.
```

**Two sentences is a floor, not a target.** The first says what the record is;
the second says something a reader could not have guessed — when one comes into
existence, what distinguishes it from the entity it sounds like, what breaks if
it is wrong. An entity help that would read the same for any business is one
nobody needed.

Every entity should have one. An entity without `help` signals to a reader that
the manual was generated from a model that did not invest in documentation — the
rest of the manual is still correct, but the opening paragraph is absent.

#### Writing an attribute's `help` — guidance for language models

Write one or two sentences that answer: *what business purpose does this field
serve, and what value is expected here?*

Rules of thumb:
- **Do not restate the field name.** "The customer email address" adds nothing to
  a field called `email`. Instead, explain what it is used for:
  `email` → *The primary contact address for invoices and automated status updates. Must be unique per account.*
- **Name the business event, not the data type.** "A date" is useless. "The date
  a signed copy was received from the counterparty" tells a user why it matters.
- **Explain enum values inline when they carry policy.**
  `Order.status` → *draft — editable; confirmed — locked for fulfilment; shipped — triggers customer notification; cancelled — terminates the order.*
- **Describe FK fields in business terms.**
  `Invoice.account_id` → *The company being billed. Must be an approved account; changing it after dispatch requires manager approval.*
- **Mention rules attached to the field.** If a workflow fires when a status
  changes to `approved`, say so: the manual is the only place that connection is
  explained in plain language outside the rules editor.

An attribute's `help` has two consumers: the form (printed as hint text beneath the
control) and the manual (the Purpose column). Writing it once covers both.

**Help is where the domain knowledge goes, and nothing else in the model carries
it.** The ERD says an entity has a `household_id`; only help says that a
membership belongs to a family and that the family's screen is where it is read.
Everything else in a model is structural — types, keys, cardinalities, states,
roles — and structure is the half a reader can already see. Help is the half
that has to be *known*: what the business calls this, why it keeps it, what
depends on it, what goes wrong when it is wrong. Write it from the research and
the brief, in the business's own vocabulary, at the level of detail somebody
joining the company would need.

This is the test to apply to every line before delivering: **could this sentence
have been written without knowing anything about the business?** If yes, it is
not help.

```
Bad:   HouseholdMember.household_id  help: Household id for HouseholdMember.
Good:  HouseholdMember.household_id  help: The family this membership is in. Listed inside the household's own screen — a membership away from its household is not something anybody looks up.

Bad:   Address                       help: Address is a business record in the platform.
Good:  Address                       help: A postal address belonging to a party, kept as its own record because a party has several — registered, correspondence, often an overseas one — and because a change of address is a KYC event that has to be evidenced rather than typed over the old one.

Bad:   Holding.average_cost          help: Average cost for Holding.
Good:  Holding.average_cost          help: The weighted average price paid per unit across the lots making up this position. It is what an unrealised gain is computed against when lots are not being tracked individually.
```

The first of each pair would pass any coverage check and leaves the reader
exactly where they started. **Three codes report the three ways a model fails
here, all warnings:**

| Code | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `EML152` | an entity carries no `help` at all |
| `EML153` | an entity has columns with no `help` — reported once per entity, naming them |
| `EML151` | help that restates its own subject instead of describing it |

`EML151` catches three shapes: `Unique identifier for X`, the column name in
prose (`Status for Client`), and a template sentence (`X is a business record in
…`). It is deliberately narrow, so real help that happens to be short — *The day
this offer expires.* — does not fire. It exists because coverage can be complete
and the help still worthless: a published model once carried help on all 91
entities and all 551 columns, of which 699 lines were of exactly these shapes.

**The primary key needs no help, and `EML153` does not ask for any.** It is a
generated uuid, read-only on every form, and the only sentence anybody could
write about it restates its name — which is what `EML151` then reports. Leave it
out.

**What to say, per kind of column:**

| Column | Say |
|---|---|
| A reference (`_id`) | what the reference is *for* — "the ward this bed stands in", never "the ward id" |
| An enum-bound column | what each value means to the business, because the dictionary lists the values and nothing says what choosing one *does* |
| A lifecycle column | which moves are possible from which state — the state machine enforces a topology no form can show |
| A money column | gross or net, which currency, and what it is compared against |
| A date | which business event it records, and what is true before it is set |
| A flag | what turning it on permits or prevents, and who may do so |

### 5.7 Document reports (AnkaReport)

Every generated application includes a document report subsystem. One default
AnkaReport layout is **seeded automatically for every entity** at generation
time — no EML directive required. Administrators can customise layouts; users
can print records.

#### The `sys_report_designs` table

| Column | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | UUID | Primary key |
| `table_name` | VARCHAR | UNIQUE — one design per entity table |
| `name` | VARCHAR | Human-readable name, e.g. "Contact Default Report" |
| `layout` | JSONB | AnkaReport `ILayout` object |

#### Default layout

Seeded by `seeds/06_report_designs.ts` (generated from
`packages/generator/templates/common/seeds/report-designs.ts.hbs`).

- **Header** — entity display name + " Report" in 20pt bold navy
- **Content** — one label/value row per field; excludes `id`, `created_at`,
  `updated_at`, `deleted_at`, `version`, and the primary key
- **Footer** — "Generated by APPWITHAI" in 9pt grey

Uses `ON CONFLICT (table_name) DO NOTHING` so regeneration never overwrites an
administrator's customisation.

#### Admin surface — Report Designs

`/admin/reports` — lists every entity table with an **Designed** (emerald) or
**New** (grey) badge.

`/admin/reports/:tableName` — opens the AnkaReport designer pre-loaded with the
existing layout. The designer's save button calls
`PUT /api/sys/report-designs/:tableName`.

#### Print button

The record toolbar (`ADToolbar`) shows a **Print** button (violet styling) in
the detail view **only** when a design exists for the current entity. Clicking
it opens `ReportPrintModal`, which:

1. Calls `AnkaReport.render()` with `data = { ...record, records: [record] }`
2. Offers an **Export PDF** button (`renderer.exportToPdf(filename)`)

The button is invisible when no design exists — no broken print experience.

#### Backend endpoints

All under `/api/sys/report-designs`, admin-only for writes:

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/sys/report-designs` | list all designs |
| `GET` | `/sys/report-designs/:tableName` | get design by table |
| `POST` | `/sys/report-designs` | create |
| `PUT` | `/sys/report-designs/:tableName` | upsert |
| `DELETE` | `/sys/report-designs/:tableName` | delete |

#### What the model controls

Nothing. Report designs are automatic. The model author does not write anything
in the model to enable or configure them. Default layouts are seeded from
the entity's column list; customisation is done through the Admin UI at runtime.

---

## 6. The modelling tool (`packages/web`)

Port 3000. TanStack Start on Vite 8, React 19, Tailwind v4, Zustand.

Wizard steps are declared **once** in `packages/web/src/types/project.ts`
(`ProjectStep`, `STEP_ORDER`, `STEP_LABELS`, `STEP_ROUTES`); `ProgressStepper`
derives itself from them.

```
init → design → logic → generate → enhance → deploy
```

- **init** — natural language in; agents domain → entity → relationship → model document
- **design** — HITL ERD approval, `ErdFlowViewer`
- **logic** — rules *and* workflows on one screen (a rule decides, a process
  acts on what it decided; they were two steps and that ordering does not exist)
- **automations** (`/projects/$id/automations`, alongside the wizard) —
  trigger → conditions → steps builder, plus rule tables
- **generate** — SSE progress
- **enhance**, **deploy**

### API route pattern

```typescript
import { createFileRoute } from "@tanstack/react-router";

export const Route = createFileRoute("/api/projects/$id")({
  server: {
    handlers: {
      GET: async ({ request, params }) => {
        const access = await requireProjectAccess(request, params.id, "read");
        if ("response" in access) return access.response;
        const { getDatabase } = await import("@appwithai/core/services");  // lazy: Node-only
        const db = getDatabase();
        const project = await db.selectFrom("projects").selectAll()
          .where("id", "=", params.id).executeTakeFirst();
        return new Response(JSON.stringify(project), {
          headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        });
      },
    },
  },
});
```

Rules: dynamic-`import()` server-only deps inside the handler; always return a
real `Response` with an explicit `Content-Type`; call `requireProjectAccess` on
anything touching a project; do **not** use the deprecated `createAPIFileRoute`.

### The automation model

`packages/web/src/lib/automation/model.ts` — one sentence, three parts: a
**trigger**, a flat list of **conditions** that must all pass, and an ordered
list of **steps**. Deliberately not a graph: the executor runs steps in order
and stops at the first failure.

Triggers are the lifecycle hooks the generated services already fire —
`created`/`beforeCreated`/`updated`/`beforeUpdated`/`deleted`/`beforeDeleted`,
mapped to `afterCreate`/`beforeCreate`/… `automationToYaml` (`lib/automation/yaml.ts`)
writes each automation as its own YAML document, `automation: "1.0"`, into
`sys_workflow_definitions.definition_yaml`; `automationFromYaml` reads it back and
refuses any other shape.

### One reader

The editors in the web app read and write the model through the same YAML reader
the generators use (`@appwithai/generator/model-yaml`), so what an editor shows
is what generation reads. A diagram the designer draws is drawn from the
document; an edit made on a diagram is an edit to the document.

---

## 7. Shared types

```typescript
// packages/core/src/types/entity.types.ts
interface Entity {
  name: string;
  tableName: string;
  attributes: EntityAttribute[];
  indexes?: EntityIndex[];      // an entity's indexes
  audited?: boolean;
  softDelete?: boolean;
}

// packages/generator/src/pipeline/generate-application.ts
interface ParsedModel {
  entities: Entity[];
  relationships: Relationship[];
  categories: EntityCategory[];   // categories
  enums: EntityEnum[];            // enums + an attribute's enum
  rules: CompiledRule[];          // rules
  hooks: CompiledHook[];          // hooks
  workflows: CompiledWorkflow[];  // stateMachines
  sagas: CompiledSaga[];          // sagas
}

// packages/generator/src/rules/index.ts
interface CompiledRuleAction {
  name: string;
  type: string;                   // trigger-workflow | validation-error | …
  when: string;                   // Zen expression; "true" fires on every write
  props: Record<string, string>;
}
```

Load the language definition through the typed accessor, never by re-parsing:

```typescript
import { loadLanguageDefinition, normalizeType, cardinalityKind, isHookType }
  from "../language";

normalizeType("varchar");    // "string"
cardinalityKind("||--o{");   // "oneToMany"
isHookType("beforeCreate");  // true
```

---

## 8. Environment and operations

### Commands

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `bun install` | dependencies (**never npm/pnpm/npx — use bun/bunx**) |
| `bun run dev` | modelling tool, :3000 |
| `bun run dev:mastra` | Mastra AI service, :4111 |
| `./scripts/start-llm.sh` | local OpenAI-compatible model, :8000 |
| `bun run type-check` | repo TypeScript |
| `bun run type-check:language` | `language/` (own config: Bun-style `.ts` imports) |
| `bun run lint:fix` | Biome check + autofix |
| `bun run test` | Vitest — 540 passing, 6 skipped, across core/generator/ai/web |
| `appwithai validate <f.eml.yaml>` | validate a model — YAML, schema, checker, at YAML lines |
| `bun run eml validate -i <f.eml.yaml>` | the same, through the `eml` CLI; `generate` applies the eight auto-repairs first |
| `bun run build:language-tools` | rebuild `html/model-yaml.js`, the published validator (§10.3) |
| `bun run test:language-tools` | assert it is current |
| `bun run check:language-bundle` | run it over every model in headless Chromium and compare with the CLI |
| `bun run parity` | generate every corpus model with both generators (and the WASM build) and diff the backends; compare the two CEDM lowerings |
| `bun run build:wasm` / `bun run wasm …` | build the Rust generator for `wasm32-wasip1`, and run it on Node's WASI |
| `bun scripts/sites/build-site-bundles.ts --check` | in the `app-with-ai-rust` copy: are the website's bundles current? |

The `--check` variants compare a committed artifact against a fresh build, byte
for byte. Bundles are `Bun.build` output, whose bytes depend on the bun version
**and** the platform, so a mismatch does not always mean "you forgot to
rebuild". CI pins bun on `linux-x64` for exactly this reason; building
elsewhere produces a variant that looks right locally and is byte-wrong for CI.

**Known-broken**, do not recommend: `bun run build && bun run start`. With a
reachable `DATABASE_URL` the built server loads `@ag-ui/mcp-apps-middleware`,
which `require()`s the ESM-only `eventsource` through the MCP SDK; Bun refuses,
and the server answers 204 to everything including `/api/health`. Use
`bun run dev`.

The scripts that used to be listed here — `migrate`, `test:app`, `test:e2e`,
`test:generator`, `test:complete`, the root `vitest.config.ts` and
`packages/web`'s eslint `lint` — have been removed rather than documented. They
pointed at files that do not exist.

### Environment variables

**AI** (`packages/ai/src/config.ts` is the only place model config lives — never
hard-code a model string or base URL): `LOCAL_AI_BASE_URL`
(`http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1`), `LOCAL_AI_MODEL`
(`mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit`), `LOCAL_AI_API_KEY`,
`LOCAL_AI_EMBEDDING_MODEL` (`bge-small-en-v1.5`),
`LOCAL_AI_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS` (384 — the pgvector column width; changing the
model means changing this **and** re-ingesting).

`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is **dead config**; `@anthropic-ai/sdk` is vestigial.

**Database**: `DATABASE_URL`, or `PGHOST`/`PGPORT`/`PGUSER`/`PGPASSWORD`/
`PGDATABASE`. Connection config lives only in
`packages/core/src/config/db.config.ts`. **pgvector is required** — retrieval
does `CREATE EXTENSION vector`; CI uses `pgvector/pgvector:pg18`.

**Web**: client vars must be `VITE_`-prefixed. Server handlers use
`process.env`.

**Security**: `SESSION_SECRET`, `JWT_SECRET`, `DB_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (base64, 32
bytes — rotating it invalidates every stored project connection).

**Generated app runtime config**: in a generated application, AI config
(`AI_BASE_URL`, `AI_API_KEY`, `AI_EMBEDDING_MODEL`, `AI_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS`),
feature toggles (`ELECTRIC_URL`, `IMMUDB_ENABLED`, `AUDIT_READS`,
`ENABLE_MODEL_CONTEXT`), rate limiting (`THROTTLE_TTL`, `THROTTLE_LIMIT`),
logging (`LOG_LEVEL`, `LOG_PRETTY`), and CORS (`CORS_ORIGIN`) can also be
managed from the database via the `sys_system` table, making the `.env` entries
optional for those settings. Bootstrap variables (`DATABASE_URL`,
`BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, `PORT`, `HOST`, `NODE_ENV`) cannot move to the database.

### CI

| Workflow | Does |
|---|---|
| `parity.yml` | type-check, generator unit tests, the Rust generator's format/clippy/test, the backend parity gate, the language bundles' currency, and the YAML bundle in a real browser |
| `project-git.yml` | the modelling tool's per-project Git history against a real Postgres |
| `validate.yml` | the CEDM specification: schema, dictionary coverage, help, enumerations |
| `enrich-entity-help.yml` | fills gaps in CEDM entity help and commits them |

**Clippy is only a gate on CI's toolchain.** `parity.yml` uses the moving
`stable` toolchain, so a lint added since the local one passes here and fails
there; run `cargo +<CI's version> clippy -p appwithai-gen --all-targets -- -D
warnings` before pushing Rust changes.

### Known security limits — state these plainly if asked

- `packages/web/src/lib/password.ts` is a **fixed-salt SHA-256**: fast to
  brute-force, identical passwords hash identically. Kept because stored hashes
  are already in this format; replacing it needs a rehash-on-login migration.
- The rate limiter is **in-memory, single-process**; counters reset on restart.
  Redis before running more than one instance.
- `requireProjectAccess` is the shared authorization helper, but
  `api/projects/$id/index.ts` still carries a local copy.

---

## 9. Worked example — building a CRM

Mirrors the human guide at https://www.appwithai.org/guide/index.html. Model:
`language/yaml/examples/crm.eml.yaml`.

**Scale**: 1 model file · 17 entities · 7 categories · 26 enums · 20 indexes ·
8 rules · 5 actions · 38 hooks · 5 state machines · 5 sagas (29 steps) ·
32 access rules · 33 authored reports → **~480 generated files**.

### 9.1 The skeleton — three entities of the seventeen

```yaml
eml: "1.0"
name: Enterprise CRM
version: 1.0.0

enums:
  - name: UserRole
    values: [administrator, sales_rep, marketing_manager]
  - name: LeadStatus
    values: [new, working, qualified, converted, disqualified]
  - name: LeadSource
    values: [web, referral, event, partner]
  - name: LeadRating
    values: [hot, warm, cold]

categories:
  - name: Marketing
    description: Campaigns and the leads they generate
    icon: Megaphone
    entities: [Campaign, Lead]
  - name: Administration
    description: The people who use the application
    icon: Settings
    entities: [User]

entities:
  - name: User
    help: Someone who signs in and does the work — a rep, a manager, a marketer. Every business record names one as its owner.
    attributes:
      - { name: id, type: string, pk: true }
      - name: email
        type: email
        unique: true
        help: The address this user signs in with. It must be unique across the application.
      - name: full_name
        type: string
        help: The name shown on screen and in email.
      - name: role
        type: string
        enum: UserRole
        help: What this user is allowed to do. The role decides which records they can see at all.
  - name: Campaign
    help: A marketing programme with a budget and a window, run to generate leads.
    attributes:
      - { name: id, type: string, pk: true }
      - name: name
        type: string
        help: What this programme is called in reporting.
      - name: start_date
        type: date
        help: The day the campaign goes live.
      - name: budgeted_cost
        type: decimal
        optional: true
        help: What marketing agreed to spend on this programme.
  - name: Lead
    help: An unqualified enquiry that has not been connected to an account yet. A lead is either converted or disqualified.
    audited: true
    attributes:
      - { name: id, type: string, pk: true }
      - name: company_name
        type: string
        help: The company they said they were from. It becomes the account name on conversion.
      - name: employee_count
        type: int
        optional: true
        help: Head count as the lead reported it; the largest single input to the score.
      - name: lead_source
        type: string
        enum: LeadSource
        help: Where the enquiry came from. Referrals score highest.
      - name: score
        type: int
        optional: true
        help: The qualification score, 0 to 100, computed when the lead is captured.
      - name: rating
        type: string
        enum: LeadRating
        optional: true
        help: Hot, warm or cold, read off the score so a rep can sort the queue at a glance.
      - name: status
        type: string
        enum: LeadStatus
        help: Where this lead has got to, from new through to converted or disqualified.
      - name: campaign_id
        type: string
        fk: true
        optional: true
        help: The campaign that produced this lead, when one did.
      - name: owner_id
        type: string
        fk: true
        help: The user working this lead.
    indexes:
      - columns: [owner_id, status]

relationships:
  - { from: Campaign, fromCardinality: exactly-one, to: Lead, toCardinality: zero-or-more, label: generates }
  - { from: User, fromCardinality: exactly-one, to: Lead, toCardinality: zero-or-more, label: owns }

stateMachines:
  - name: LeadLifecycle
    entity: Lead
    title: Lead Lifecycle
    states: [new, working, qualified, converted, disqualified]
    initial: new
    final: [converted, disqualified]
    transitions:
      - { from: new, to: working, trigger: start_work }
      - { from: working, to: qualified, trigger: qualify }
      - { from: working, to: disqualified, trigger: disqualify }
      - { from: qualified, to: converted, trigger: convert }

rules:
  - name: leadScoring
    title: Lead Scoring
    entity: Lead
    event: beforeCreate
    priority: 10
    nodes:
      - { id: A, label: "Start: Lead Captured", type: start }
      - { id: B, label: employee_count >= 1000?, type: decision }
      - { id: C, label: Add 35 firmographic points, type: expression }
      - { id: D, label: Add 5 firmographic points, type: expression }
      - { id: E, label: Compute lead score, type: function }
      - { id: Z, label: "End: Lead Scored", type: end }
    edges:
      - { from: A, to: B }
      - { from: B, to: C, label: "Yes" }
      - { from: B, to: D, label: "No" }
      - { from: C, to: E }
      - { from: D, to: E }
      - { from: E, to: Z }
  - name: leadQualification
    title: Lead Qualification
    entity: Lead
    event: beforeUpdate
    priority: 15
    nodes:
      - { id: A, label: "Start: Lead Updated", type: start }
      - { id: B, label: status == qualified?, type: decision }
      - { id: Z, label: "End: Lead Routed", type: end }
    edges:
      - { from: A, to: B }
      - { from: B, to: Z, label: "Yes" }
      - { from: B, to: Z, label: "No" }
    actions:
      - name: convertQualifiedLead
        type: trigger-workflow
        when: status == "qualified"
        props:
          workflow: LeadConversion
          message: Lead qualified — converting it

sagas:
  - name: LeadConversion
    title: Lead Conversion
    entity: Lead
    trigger: rule
    steps:
      - id: B
        type: UpdateEntity
        label: Mark the lead converted
        properties:
          field: status
          value: converted

rbac:
  - entity: Campaign
    action: read
    roles: [marketing_manager]
  - entity: Lead
    action: read
    roles: [sales_rep, marketing_manager]
  - entity: Lead
    action: convert
    roles: [sales_rep]
```

That is a complete model, not an excerpt: it validates with no diagnostics and
generates a running application. The full CRM grows it to seventeen entities, but
the shape does not change. One file, one document. Every construct sits under its
own key, so an entity's whole behaviour — its columns, its rules, its lifecycle,
who may touch it — is found by its name rather than by position.

### 9.2–9.3 Rules and workflows

Covered in §3.2–§3.3. A rule is bound by its `entity`, `event` and `priority`:
`leadScoring` runs on `Lead` at `beforeCreate` with priority 10 — its name
appears in the Business Rules screen and is how a saga step can reference the
rule instead of copying its table; the entity must be declared; the event is any
of the 13 hook events (`before*` can still block the write); the priority orders
rules on the same entity and event, lower first.

### 9.4 Generate

```bash
appwithai validate language/yaml/examples/crm.eml.yaml
#   crm.eml.yaml  0 errors · 0 warnings

bun run generate:tanstack -- -i language/yaml/examples/crm.eml.yaml \
  -o generated-projects/crm -n crm --no-setup --force
```

The generator runs the same validation itself; running it first is instant and
tells you the truth before anything is written. It prints entities and attribute
counts, then the rules, hooks, sagas, state machines and categories it compiled.

The browser designer is the better first path — it draws the ERD from the
document, validates as you type, and keeps versions. Both call the same
pipeline, so both produce the same application.

### 9.5–9.6 The application, and the dictionary

Nothing on the screens was designed for the CRM specifically. The dashboard is
seven blocks for the seven `categories`; every entity gets the same list
(search, sortable columns, pagination, New, a Help chip) drawn from the
dictionary's field definitions.

**The fastest feedback loop in the system**: rename a category or move an entity
between groups in the model, regenerate, re-seed, reload — the dashboard
reorganises. If users cannot find things, that is a modelling fix, not a
front-end one.

### 9.7 Watch it run — the chain end to end

One user action, eight links, every one of them declared in the model:

| # | What runs | Declared as |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | a user sets `status = qualified` | a value of the `LeadStatus` enum |
| 2 | `leadQualification` evaluates | `rules: [{ name: leadQualification, entity: Lead, event: beforeUpdate }]` |
| 3 | its action fires | `actions: [{ type: trigger-workflow, when: status == "qualified", props: { workflow: LeadConversion } }]` |
| 4 | `LeadConversion` starts | `sagas: [{ name: LeadConversion, trigger: rule }]` |
| 5 | a decision table sizes the account | step `B`, `type: Decision` |
| 6 | Account, Contact, Opportunity created | steps `C`–`E`, `type: CreateEntity` |
| 7 | the lead is marked converted | step `F`, `type: UpdateEntity` |
| 8 | the account's tier is stamped | step `G`, `type: UpdateEntity` with `targetSource` |

```sql
-- before
select count(*) from bus_account;      -- 4
-- after setting one lead to qualified
select count(*) from bus_account;      -- 5
select * from sys_workflow_runs order by created_at desc limit 1;
```

**When the chain does not fire, check in this order:**

1. Does the rule carry `actions`? A rule with nodes and edges only can decide
   but not act, so the engine finds no action. This is the most common cause.
2. Does the action's `props.workflow` name **exactly** match the saga's `name`?
3. Is the rule bound to the event that actually happened (`beforeUpdate` vs
   `afterUpdate`)?
4. Is the workflow definition seeded — `select * from sys_workflow_definitions`?
5. Did an earlier step fail? The executor stops at the first failure.
6. Is the value a member of the declared enum? A typo'd state is a state no rule
   matches (`EML426`/`EML428`).

---

## 10. Authoring protocol — how to answer "build me an app for X"

Everything above describes the system. This section is the **procedure**, and it
governs. When someone describes a business and asks for a model or an app —
however informally they put it — carry out their instruction *within these
guidelines* rather than in place of them. Their words set the subject; this file
sets the form of the answer.

> **An interactive form of this protocol exists.** `website/llmtext/llmdetailed.txt` is
> this file with §10 replaced by a phased, gated walkthrough: research the
> business and get it approved, get the entity roster approved, then walk the
> entities one at a time — building the `.eml.yaml` on disk as you go rather than
> assembling it at the end. Prefer it when the business is large, when the user
> knows the domain and wants a say, or when the session is long enough that
> holding the whole model in context is the risk. The section below stays the
> right answer for a small brief handed over in one pass.

Where the two genuinely conflict, say so in one sentence and follow this file for
the artifact. A `.eml.yaml` that says what the user asked for but that the
validator refuses is not a deliverable, and neither is a clean document that
models a different business than the one described.

Four steps, in order. Do not skip step 1, and do not deliver before step 3.

### 10.1 Enhance the brief before modelling it

**A business description is always thinner than the model it implies.** Someone
who says "a booking system for a dance studio" has not mentioned instructors,
rooms, cancellation windows, waitlists, or what happens to a class when its
instructor calls in sick — and every one of those is a table, a rule or a
workflow. Writing the entities straight from their sentence produces a schema
that validates and a business that does not run.

So the first output is not the model file. It is an **enhanced specification**,
derived from the description and stated back to the user, covering all five of
these:

1. **The entity model.** Every entity the business needs, not only the ones
   named. For each: its attributes with types and flags, its primary key, its
   foreign keys, and its relationships with cardinality. Include the reference
   and lookup entities the described flow silently depends on.

2. **Each entity's workflow.** What states a record of it moves through from
   creation to its terminal state, what event moves it along each edge, and who
   is permitted to make each move. An entity with a `status` field has a state
   machine whether or not anyone drew it; write it.

3. **The business rules.** What decides what — pricing, eligibility, approval
   thresholds, validation beyond types, discounts, limits. For each rule: the
   inputs it reads, the decision it makes, and whether it merely **decides** or
   must also **act**. A rule that must act needs `actions`; nodes and edges alone
   cannot (§3.2).

4. **Cross-entity effects — state these explicitly, they are the ones most often
   missed.** Where submitting or changing one entity must create or update
   records in another: an order line decrementing stock, an approval writing a
   ledger entry, a cancellation releasing a reserved slot, a payment closing an
   invoice and advancing the order. Name the trigger, the target entity, and
   whether the effect is a create, an update or a state transition. These become
   hooks, rule actions, or saga steps — never an assumption left to the reader.

5. **The multi-step workflows.** Any business flow that spans more than one
   entity or more than one actor, defined end to end: every step, its order, the
   entity each step touches, what happens when a step fails, and what compensates
   a step already taken. A flow left at "and then it gets fulfilled" generates an
   application that cannot fulfil anything. Model these as `sagas` with typed
   `steps` (§3.3).

State assumptions as assumptions. Where the description leaves a genuine fork —
two plausible businesses, materially different models — ask, rather than picking
silently. Where it leaves an ordinary gap, fill it the way a careful analyst
would and say what you filled.

### 10.2 Write the model

Only now write the document, following §3 in full: the `entities` and
`relationships`, the `rules`, the `stateMachines` and `sagas`, and the keys that
give them meaning. Every entity from 10.1 appears; every rule from 10.1 is an
entry in `rules`, with `actions` where it must act; every cross-entity effect
from 10.1 is a hook, an action or a step; every multi-step flow is a saga.

Name the file after the business: **`<business-name>.eml.yaml`** — lower-case,
hyphenated, no spaces (`acme-dance-studio.eml.yaml`). One file, opening with
`eml: "1.0"`.

Check a construct's status before relying on it (§3.0). A construct the schema
accepts but no compiler reads will not change a generated application, so do
not promise the user behaviour that rides on it.

**Three things are not optional, and each is usually what is missing when a
model checks clean and the application still disappoints:**

- **`description` at the top** — a multi-sentence summary of what the
  application does. Not a tagline. This populates the generated manual, the
  `sys_system.APP_DESCRIPTION` config row, and the admin dashboard header.
- **Help on every entity and every column, and it has to be domain knowledge**
  (§3.1, §5.6). An entity's `help` for each entity, an attribute's `help` for
  each column except the primary key. Clear every `EML151`, `EML152` and
  `EML153`: the first means a line restates its own name rather than describing
  it, and it is the one that survives a coverage check. No exceptions, including
  the obvious ones. This is the only explanation the generated application will
  ever have, and nobody adds it afterwards.
- **Line items declared as such** (§3.1). Go through the entities and ask of
  each: is this a thing in its own right, or part of another thing? Every
  invoice line, order line, prescription item, delivery line and answer-to-a-
  question gets `parent: <Parent>`, and is left out of `categories`. Missing it
  puts a screen on the dashboard listing every line ever written, which is a
  screen nobody opens — and leaves the parent record with no sign of its own
  lines. The checker reports every candidate it can see as `EML149`; walk each
  one and either declare the parent or decide against it.

### 10.3 Validate against the published validator — three runs, three repairs

The model is not finished when it is written. It is finished when the validator
accepts it.

**If you have a shell, this is the whole step** — no checkout, no Bun, nothing
installed:

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/check-model.mjs
node check-model.mjs model.eml.yaml
#   exit 0  clean · exit 1  the generator would refuse it · exit 2  it could not run
```

`check-model.mjs` runs the three passes below against the published validator
and prints its report, every finding at its YAML line and column, the verdict
last. `--write` saves the repairs it applied; `--base <dir-or-url>` points it at
another copy.

**A clean report is not a finished model, and there is a second runner for
that.** Nothing in the checker requires a model to *have* anything: one entity
with a primary key and a name is a valid model with no lifecycle, no rule, no
access control and not one word of help text — zero errors, zero warnings, which
is true and is not the same as *this model is done*.

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs
node audit-model.mjs model.eml.yaml
#   exit 0  every check passed · exit 1  one or more failed · exit 2  it could not run
```

It scores the file contract and the delivery checklist mechanically —
twenty-two checks, last line `22 passed, 0 failed`: a primary key per entity,
`fk` on every reference column, an enum binding behind every status, a state
machine with an initial and a final state, rule `actions`, `hooks`, `sagas` and
`rbac` all present, help on every entity and every column that is not a
restatement of its own name, every declared line item out of every category, and
the three validator passes over the file's own bytes. `--quiet` prints the score
alone; `--base` is the same flag, so the offline rungs below apply unchanged.

**It is a scorer, not a second checker** — every diagnostic it reads comes from
`model-yaml.js`, and it adds no codes of its own. Run both, and report both.

| File | URL | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `guide/model-yaml.js` | `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js` | the reader, the schema and the checker as `validate(text)`, and the eight auto-repairs as `fix(text)` — repair and re-check in one call |
| `guide/check-model.mjs` | `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/check-model.mjs` | the three passes below, as a command |
| `guide/audit-model.mjs` | `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs` | the twenty-two-point audit |

`model-yaml.js` is an ES module bundled from the language's own reader,
schema, checker and fixer. It is the same engine the CLI runs, not a lighter web
edition, so a document that passes here is a document `appwithai` will accept.

**A checkout is not required, and neither is Bun.** The CLI is the convenient
path when this repository is already on disk; it is not the authoritative one,
and nothing downstream distinguishes a verdict that came from it. In particular
— and this has been observed in the wild — **failing to reach GitHub says
nothing about whether the validator can run.** The modules are served from
`https://www.appwithai.org`, and `check-model.mjs` resolves them from `--base`,
then from its own directory, then from the published site. GitHub is in none of
those paths. "I could not obtain the repository, therefore I could not
validate" is a wrong inference, not an honest limitation.

**The same mistake generalises.** Not reaching GitHub, not reaching
`llmdetailed.txt` itself, and Node refusing a URL import are each one address or
one call failing. None of them is a statement about `guide/model-yaml.js`, which
is a different file on a different host — and `check-model.mjs` needs no
specification document at all: it reads the model and nothing else. Whatever you
could not fetch, walk the ladder before reporting the validator as unavailable.

**Perform the validation; do not offer it.** "If you want the actual counts, I
can run the published validator" hands the user a choice they were never given:
the run is required, so the counts are part of the deliverable rather than an
upgrade to it.

**Retry down the ladder before you conclude anything.** One failed attempt is a
finding about that attempt, not about the environment. Stop at the first rung
that runs:

| # | Rung | When it applies |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `appwithai validate <file>` or `bun run eml validate -i <file>` | this repository is already on disk |
| 2 | `curl -sO …/check-model.mjs`, then `node check-model.mjs <file>` | any shell with Node 18+, Bun or Deno — **this is the rung that answers "I could not clone the repository"** |
| 3 | `fetch` the module into a directory and `import()` it | a runtime that can make a request but has no `curl`. Node has no network imports: a URL `import` there fails with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_ESM_URL_SCHEME`, which reads like the module being unreachable rather than like Node declining that form |
| 4 | `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/11-check-a-model.html` | no shell at all. It runs the same module in the tab, so if you can drive or render a browser this is a real run and its counts are reportable |
| 5 | The by-hand list below | only once 1–4 have actually been tried and failed |

```js
import { validate, fix } from "https://www.appwithai.org/guide/model-yaml.js";

let model = /* the .eml.yaml you just wrote */;

// Pass 1 — repair the auto-fixable codes, keeping comments, then re-check.
let result = fix(model);
model = result.text;

// Passes 2 and 3 — check the repaired bytes, and confirm they are stable.
for (let pass = 2; pass <= 3 && result.ok; pass++) {
  result = { ...validate(model), text: model };
}
```

**Iterate until clean — at least 10 cycles.** Run the validator, apply the fixer,
correct every remaining diagnostic in the YAML, re-run. Repeat this cycle **at
least 10 times** or until the report shows zero errors and zero warnings —
whichever comes first. A single pass is never enough — a repair can uncover a
problem the original error was masking.

**Fix the complete file across all iterations.** Each cycle must address every
diagnostic — errors and warnings alike. Read the diagnostic: each carries a
`code`, a `line`, a `column` and usually a `hint`, and the codes are banded so
the band tells you where the fault is (§3.0). Fix the cause in the model, not
the symptom in the text, and check again.

Do not deliver a document that still has diagnostics after 10 correction
attempts. If diagnostics persist after all 10 iterations, deliver the best
version you have, say plainly which diagnostics remain and what you tried, and
let the user decide. Silently shipping a model that fails validation is the one
outcome worse than not finishing.

**Warnings are not noise** (§3.0). Most describe something the generator accepts
and quietly gets wrong — a dropped constraint, a state no enum backs, a rule that
can decide but cannot act. Clear them, or say why you left one.

**If rung 5 is where you land** — no shell, no network, no JavaScript engine —
that changes what you may *claim*, not what you deliver. Walk this table against
the file's actual text. Each row names the diagnostic it prevents, so a report
the user gets later is traceable to a line you did or did not check.

| Read your file and confirm | Code it prevents |
|---|---|
| It opens with `eml: "1.0"` and declares at least one entity under `entities` | schema |
| `name` is present | `EML001` |
| Every entity declares exactly one attribute with `pk: true` | `EML117` |
| Every `fk: true` column ends `_id` | `EML114` |
| Every foreign key resolves to a declared entity **by name** — `purchase_order_line_id` finds `PurchaseOrderLine`, and finds nothing if the entity is called `POLine` — or names it with `references` | `EML118` `EML502` |
| Every foreign key has a matching entry in `relationships` | `EML502` |
| Every type appears in §3.4 | schema |
| Every attribute's `enum` names a declared enum | `EML144` |
| Every state machine has `initial` and `final` | `EML421` `EML422` |
| Every state is a value of the enum bound to that status column | `EML426` `EML428` |
| Every `rbac` entry, rule, state machine, saga and hook names a declared entity | `EML213` `EML307` `EML400` `EML202` |
| Every `rbac` action is a CRUD operation or a transition that entity's machine declares | `EML214` |
| Every saga with `trigger: rule` is named by some rule action | `EML286` |

Then hand the file over with one plain sentence: the validator could not be run
here, this is what was verified by hand, and the user can validate it in their
own browser in seconds at
`https://www.appwithai.org/guide/11-check-a-model.html`. Never report a check of
your own devising in the vocabulary of a validator result — "passes", "0
warnings", a pass count — because the reader cannot tell the two apart. An
unvalidated `.eml.yaml` delivered with that sentence is still the deliverable; a
hedge in place of one never is.

### 10.4 Deliver

**Run the loop one last time, over the exact bytes you are about to hand over.**
Editing stops; validation starts again from zero. The file that leaves your
hands must be the one that came out of a run reporting **0 errors**: not an
earlier draft, not the copy you validated before the last correction. Deliver
only when that last run is clean, or say plainly which diagnostics survived 10
cycles.

Hand back the finished `<business-name>.eml.yaml` as a **downloadable file**, not
as a fenced block the user has to copy out of a chat log. Alongside it, give:

- the enhanced specification from 10.1, so the user can see what you inferred and
  correct you where you guessed wrong;
- the final validator result — errors, warnings and infos, with counts — and the
  audit score; or, where §10.3's ladder reached rung 5, the plain statement that
  the validator was not run, what was verified by hand, and where the user can
  run it themselves;
- anything you assumed, and anything still unresolved.

The user should be able to take that one file straight to `appwithai generate`.

---

## 11. Rules for answering questions about this system

1. **Resolve which application** — the modelling tool (`packages/web`) or a
   generated app (API :3000, front end :3001)? Most ambiguity in questions about "the app" is this.
2. **Check a construct's status before promising behaviour** (§3.0). A
   construct the schema accepts and no compiler reads will not change a
   generated application. An entity's `help` is never inert: it becomes
   `sys_table.description` and the whole of the manual's prose (§5.3, §5.6).
3. **A rule that must act needs `actions`** — nodes and edges alone cannot.
4. **Never hard-code a model string or base URL.** Import from
   `packages/ai/src/config.ts`.
5. **Never add a generator input at a call site.** It goes in
   `pipeline/generate-application.ts`, once.
6. **`bun run type-check` proves nothing about templates.** Generate an app and
   build it.
7. **Do not look for per-entity UI components.** Screens come from the
   dictionary; change the model or the dictionary row.
8. **`rbac` restricts, never grants.** A target no entry names is open. If
   asked why a rule "isn't working", check in order: is the role name reaching
   the request (`sysRoles` vs Better Auth's `role`), is the caller a master
   role, and for a transition — is the record actually in the `from` state the
   rule covers?
9. **Use `bun`/`bunx`, never `npm`/`pnpm`/`npx`**, including in generated
   projects.
10. **Update `language/yaml/eml.schema.json` and `language/appwithai-language.json`
    first** when changing language semantics, then the spec, then the reader and
    the compilers — in TypeScript and Rust alike.
11. **When the definition and a compiler disagree, the compiler wins** — and the
    definition is the bug to fix.
12. **Never hand over a model you have not checked.** §10.3 — three validator
    runs, at most three correction attempts, and say plainly what remains if it
    does not come clean. Work the §10.3 ladder to its last rung before
    concluding the validator is out of reach: **a repository you could not clone
    is not a validator you could not run**, since the engine is published at
    `https://www.appwithai.org`, reachable by one `curl`, and runnable in a browser tab.
    Never describe anything but a run of the published engine as a validation
    result, and never withhold the file because you could not produce one.
